items.stem: Google Flu Trends was discontinued after it significantly overestimated flu levels in which season?

items.stem: "More data always produces more accurate predictions." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Large data sets can still be biased, unrepresentative or noisy; Google Flu Trends had vast data but overestimated flu, showing veracity and model quality matter more than size alone.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why big data can find correlations but may not explain causes.
items.answer: Analysing huge data sets reveals patterns (e.g. search terms rising with flu), but correlation does not show why; hidden factors or changes in behaviour (media coverage, algorithm changes) can break the pattern, as with Google Flu Trends. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: Using the Cambridge Analytica scandal as an example, explain the failure of informed consent.
items.answer: In 2014 an app by researcher Aleksandr Kogan collected data from Facebook users and their friends (up to 87 million people); the data was used by Cambridge Analytica for political profiling. items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that the GDPR has successfully protected the privacy of EU citizens.
items.answer: The GDPR has raised standards and given individuals rights, but uneven enforcement and consent fatigue limit its effectiveness.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large fines (Meta €1.2bn, Amazon €746m in Luxembourg 2021); new rights (access, erasure, portability); global influence (Brussels effect). Arguments against: enforcement slow and concentrated in Ireland; consent fatigue and dark patterns persist; big firms can afford compliance; small firms struggle. Supported judgement: The GDPR has raised standards and given individuals rights, but uneven enforcement and consent fatigue limit its effectiveness. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "datafication"?
options: The EU law, applied from 25 May 2018, that sets rules for processing personal data and gives individuals rights over their data
Data sets so large, fast or varied that they cannot be handled by traditional tools, often described by volume, velocity and variety
Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, an organisation that decides the purpose and means of processing personal data
Turning aspects of life that were not previously quantified (friendships, movement, sleep) into data that can be analysed (Mayer-Schönberger and Cukier)
items.answer: Turning aspects of life that were not previously quantified (friendships, movement, sleep) into data that can be analysed (Mayer-Schönberger and Cukier)
items.markingKey: D. "datafication" is turning aspects of life that were not previously quantified (friendships, movement, sleep) into data that can be analysed (Mayer-Schönberger and Cukier).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "data fiduciary"?
options: Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, an organisation that decides the purpose and means of processing personal data
The systematic monitoring of people's behaviour, communications or movements, by states, companies or others
Using historical data and statistical models to forecast future outcomes or behaviour
The right of individuals to control information about themselves and to be free from unwanted intrusion
items.answer: Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, an organisation that decides the purpose and means of processing personal data
items.markingKey: A. "data fiduciary" is under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, an organisation that decides the purpose and means of processing personal data.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "panopticon"?
options: Examining data to find patterns, relationships and trends that support decisions
Turning aspects of life that were not previously quantified (friendships, movement, sleep) into data that can be analysed (Mayer-Schönberger and Cukier)
A prison design by Jeremy Bentham in which inmates can always be watched, used by Michel Foucault as a metaphor for self-disciplining under constant possible observation
The principle that only data that is necessary for a specified purpose should be collected and kept
items.answer: A prison design by Jeremy Bentham in which inmates can always be watched, used by Michel Foucault as a metaphor for self-disciplining under constant possible observation
items.markingKey: C. "panopticon" is a prison design by Jeremy Bentham in which inmates can always be watched, used by Michel Foucault as a metaphor for self-disciplining under constant possible observation.

items.stem: "Big data is only used by technology companies." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Governments (census, tax, health), hospitals, retailers, sports teams and scientists use big data – e.g. public health agencies tracking disease or cities managing traffic.
items.markingKey: Governments (census, tax, health), hospitals, retailers, sports teams and scientists use big data – e.g. public health agencies tracking disease or cities managing traffic. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between security and privacy.
items.answer: Privacy concerns who should have access to personal data and for what purposes; security concerns protecting data from unauthorised access or damage – data can be secure yet used in privacy-invasive ways.
items.markingKey: Privacy concerns who should have access to personal data and for what purposes; security concerns protecting data from unauthorised access or damage – data can be secure yet used in privacy-invasive ways. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between targeted surveillance and mass surveillance.
items.answer: Targeted surveillance focuses on specific suspects, usually with a warrant; mass surveillance collects data on whole populations without individual suspicion.
items.markingKey: Targeted surveillance focuses on specific suspects, usually with a warrant; mass surveillance collects data on whole populations without individual suspicion. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the variety of big data creates challenges for analysis.
items.answer: Data comes in many forms – text, images, sensor readings, transactions – often unstructured and from different sources, so it must be cleaned, combined and interpreted, which is complex and can introduce errors.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Data comes in many forms – text, images, sensor readings, transactions – often unstructured and from different sources, so it must be cleaned, combined and interpreted, which is complex and can introduce errors. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "The GDPR only applies to companies based in Europe." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It applies to any organisation processing personal data of people in the EU when offering them goods or services or monitoring their behaviour, regardless of where the company is located.
items.markingKey: It applies to any organisation processing personal data of people in the EU when offering them goods or services or monitoring their behaviour, regardless of where the company is located. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why surveillance can change behaviour even when no one is actually watching.
items.answer: As in the panopticon, people who believe they might be observed adjust their behaviour – avoiding searches, protests or speech – producing a chilling effect and self-discipline without direct intervention.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: As in the panopticon, people who believe they might be observed adjust their behaviour – avoiding searches, protests or speech – producing a chilling effect and self-discipline without direct intervention. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A city's network of traffic sensors generated 8 terabytes (TB) of data in 2018 and 12 TB in 2020. Calculate the percentage increase.

Under the GDPR, the highest tier of fines is up to €20 million or 4% of a company's total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. A cloud provider has an annual turnover of €800 million. Calculate the maximum fine it could face.
items.answer: €32 million
items.markingKey: 4% of €800m = €32.0m [M1]; compare with €20m; the higher is €32 million [A1].

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Pegasus Project (2021) shows surveillance as a threat to human rights.
items.answer: A consortium of journalists and Amnesty International's Security Lab found that NSO Group's Pegasus spyware had targeted phones of journalists, activists and politicians in several countries. Zero-click spyware turned phones into tracking devices, chilling journalism and dissent and showing a market for state surveillance tools.
items.markingKey: Context (A consortium of journalists and Amnesty International's Security Lab found that NSO Group's Pegasus spyware had targeted phones of journalists, activists and politicians in several countries.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: zero-click spyware turned phones into tracking devices, chilling journalism and dissent and showing a market for state surveillance tools. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to surveillance as a threat to human rights.

items.stem: Using Google Flu Trends (2008–2015) as an example, explain the limits of big data.
items.answer: Google estimated flu levels from search queries; it worked at first but overestimated the 2012–13 season by about double and was shut down. It showed that correlations found in massive data can break down when behaviour or algorithms change, so big data needs theory and validation.
items.markingKey: Context (Google estimated flu levels from search queries; it worked at first but overestimated the 2012–13 season by about double and was shut down.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it showed that correlations found in massive data can break down when behaviour or algorithms change, so big data needs theory and validation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the limits of big data.

items.stem: Under the GDPR, the highest tier of fines is up to €20 million or 4% of a company's total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. A social-media company has an annual turnover of €300 million. Calculate the maximum fine it could face.
items.answer: €20 million
items.markingKey: 4% of €300m = €12.0m [M1]; compare with €20m; the higher is €20 million [A1].

items.stem: Police use live facial recognition at a music festival in Mumbai attended by 80,000 people. The system wrongly flags about 1 in 5,000 innocent people as a match. 5 people on the watch list attend, and the system correctly flags 90% of them. Calculate the expected number of false alerts and the percentage of all alerts that are correct.
items.answer: 16 false alerts; 22% of alerts correct

items.stem: A city's network of traffic sensors generated 25 terabytes (TB) of data in 2018. If the volume doubles every 3 years, calculate the volume after 10 years.
items.answer: 252 TB

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The GDPR has successfully protected the privacy of EU citizens."
items.answer: The GDPR has raised standards and given individuals rights, but uneven enforcement and consent fatigue limit its effectiveness.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large fines (Meta €1.2bn, Amazon €746m in Luxembourg 2021); new rights (access, erasure, portability); global influence (Brussels effect). Arguments against: enforcement slow and concentrated in Ireland; consent fatigue and dark patterns persist; big firms can afford compliance; small firms struggle. Supported judgement: The GDPR has raised standards and given individuals rights, but uneven enforcement and consent fatigue limit its effectiveness.

items.stem: "Mass surveillance is justified if it prevents terrorism." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Targeted, warrant-based surveillance can be justified, but mass surveillance is disproportionate given limited evidence of effectiveness and high rights costs.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: security agencies claim it helps detect plots; utilitarian argument: protecting many lives. Arguments against: evidence that bulk collection stopped attacks is limited (US review panels 2013–14); violates privacy of millions; risk of misuse against dissent. Supported judgement: Targeted, warrant-based surveillance can be justified, but mass surveillance is disproportionate given limited evidence of effectiveness and high rights costs. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "Big data has improved decision-making in public services." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Big data can improve decisions when combined with expert judgement, validation and privacy safeguards, but it is not automatically better.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: transport and health planning using real-time data; faster detection of outbreaks and fraud. Arguments against: bias and errors in data lead to unfair decisions; privacy concerns about secondary use; over-reliance on correlation (Google Flu Trends). Supported judgement: Big data can improve decisions when combined with expert judgement, validation and privacy safeguards, but it is not automatically better. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "Consent is the best basis for protecting personal data." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Consent matters, but on its own it is weak; rules on purpose limitation, minimisation and accountability give stronger protection.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: respects individual autonomy; easy to understand in principle. Arguments against: people cannot read hundreds of policies; consent is often not informed; power imbalance (accept or lose service); stronger limits on purpose and data minimisation may protect better. Supported judgement: Consent matters, but on its own it is weak; rules on purpose limitation, minimisation and accountability give stronger protection.
